title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Landscaping
audience: Owners of small Australian landscaping businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short visits, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A rate depends on skill, experience, the range of work offered, the plant and equipment you run and the cost of running the business. A landscaper who can design, supply, plant and build a simple structure in one job may justify a higher rate than one who plants only. Use local evidence. The Melbourne cost guide lists a landscaper at $50, $72 and $99 per hour, and a bobcat with operator at $81 to $145 per hour (What's the Damage, verified 1 November 2026). Use these as reference points. The page does not say what the hourly rates include, so treat them as rough. Do not cut your rate to win work.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Travel to sites, quoting, design time, admin, marketing, equipment upkeep, training, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid hours in a year, subtract the non-billable time and divide your costs by what remains. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours, a general range rather than an Australian figure (Jobber, 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). If only 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the rate must be about 1.67 times the fully billable rate (100 divided by 60). Quoting time is often unbilled, so count it.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add annual costs, including insurance, plant and vehicle costs, tools, materials handling, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. On-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure (business.gov.au, 1 October 2026). Confirm with a registered tax agent how leave and superannuation apply. Divide by billable hours, and review the rate about every three months (Business Victoria, undated).

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instruction.body: A short job, such as a small repair to a bed or a site visit for a quote, can cost more in time than it earns, because travel and set-up do not shrink with the job. Set a minimum that covers travel, set-up and admin, and state it before the visit. Take the full visit cost, divide it by one minus the target margin (Contractor+, 23 September 2026; figures illustrative, method only). For example, a full visit cost of $40 (illustrative) at a 30 per cent margin gives a minimum of $57.14. Design fees are a separate matter: the cost guide's garden design range of $720 to $4,500 is a market reference for a plan, not a minimum. No sourced rule on minimum or call-out charges for Victoria was found, so check before publishing a price sheet.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, plant and vehicle, tools, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short job or quote visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative: a landscaper's log shows that only 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, but the landscaper plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate, and what should the rate be built from?
workedExamples.reasoning: The rate would come out about 40 per cent below the level the costs require, because the costs must come from 60 billable hours, not 100 (60 divided by 100 is 0.6). The landscaper builds the rate from billable hours, adds plant, vehicle and insurance costs as overheads, sets the minimum for quote visits, and checks the result against the cost guide's landscaper range before publishing the price sheet.

equipmentAndPpe: Annual costs and income worksheet with plant and vehicle lines
Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate, the design fee basis and the minimum charge

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a cost-guide figure without checking your own costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short quote visits at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. Misleading price statements are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026). The sources read for this variant do not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm how leave and superannuation apply to the owner's own pay with a registered tax agent before the rate is published.

Work that may be domestic building work in Victoria, such as decks, retaining structures and fencing, carries registered-practitioner and insurance thresholds (Victorian Building Authority, undated). Price those jobs only after checking the rules. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short job or quote visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short jobs.

knowledgeChecks.question: A landscaper can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short landscaping visits?
options: Because short visits need travel but no set-up time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly cost.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. General range, not an Australian figure. Supports: billable time typically 60 to 80 per cent of working hours.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Figures labelled illustrative; no country stated. Only the method is used.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

What's the Damage, 'Landscaping cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/landscaping-cost-melbourne/, verified 1 November 2026. Cost guide; not a regulator. Supports: landscaper $50 / $72 / $99 per hour; bobcat with operator $81 to $145 per hour; garden design $720 / $1,800 / $4,500. GST treatment not stated.

Victorian Building Authority, 'Landscaping', https://www.vba.vic.gov.au/consumers/home-renovation-essentials/landscaping, no date shown. Supports: registered practitioner threshold; insurance threshold; which work is generally not domestic building work.
